problem: A point cloud is an unordered set of n points (a network must be invariant to the N! input orders), its category and part labels must not change under rigid transformations, and per-point segmentation needs both local and global information — sorting or an RNN over a sequence does not resolve the ordering issue.

inputs: n×3 point cloud (x, y, z of n points)
outputs: k class scores for the whole shape (classification)

contributions.name: max pooling layer as a symmetric function
contributions.solves: unordered input: aggregating the per-point features h(x_i) with an element-wise max makes the global feature invariant to the order of the n points
contributions.shown_by: accent 'max pooling / symmetric function' box between the n×1024 per-point stack and the 1024-d global feature, expanded in the basic-module zoom-in (h(x_1)…h(x_n) = n×1024 in any order -> element-wise MAX -> γ -> [f_1…f_K])

contributions.name: two joint alignment networks (T-net)
contributions.solves: invariance under geometric transformations: a mini-network predicts a transformation matrix applied to the input coordinates (3×3) and to the point features (64×64, regularised towards orthogonal)
contributions.shown_by: two accent T-net boxes above the main line, each feeding a matrix-multiply glyph on it; the training-only L_reg on A beside the feature T-net

contributions.name: local and global information combination structure
contributions.solves: segmentation needs local and global knowledge: the global feature is concatenated with each point's feature before new per-point features are extracted
contributions.shown_by: accent 'local + global concat' box under the global feature, joined by the n×64 point-feature arrow from the feature alignment, leading to the n×1088 stack and per-point scores

mechanism.explains: why the network is order-invariant: the shared MLPs (h) map every point independently on the strip; the zoom-in shows the element-wise MAX over the n vectors h(x_i), which is symmetric, and γ mapping the result to the global signature [f_1, …, f_K] (Eq. 1, Theorem 1)
how alignment works: a T-net predicts a matrix that multiplies all points' coordinates (3×3) or features (A, 64×64); during training L_reg = ||I − AA^T||_F^2 keeps A close to orthogonal

color_semantics.teal: the paper's key modules (style accent; blueprint tone 'orange' = the proposed role): T-nets (joint alignment), max pooling / MAX (symmetric function), local + global combination
color_semantics.yellow: white fill with a dark outline: learned features (per-point n×d stacks, h(x_i), the global feature vector) and the L_reg box; editorial-minimal renders tones blue/red/yellow as this white fill and the grammar check names it 'yellow'
color_semantics.blue: same white fill as 'yellow' (the blueprint's tone for learned features)

annotate: n×3 input, n×64, n×1024, n×1088 per-point features
MLP widths on the arrows (from the code)
k class scores, n×m per-point scores
takeaway: PointNet maps every point with a shared MLP, after aligning points and features with T-nets, and max-pools over all points into one order-invariant global feature, which classifies the shape and, concatenated back to each point's feature, segments it.

reader_questions.glance: point cloud in, class scores and per-point scores out, through shared per-point MLPs and one max pool
reader_questions.detail: why max pooling makes the network permutation-invariant (zoom-in), and how the T-nets and the local+global concat work

why: PointNet's message has a 5-second level (points -> per-point MLP -> one max pool -> two heads) and a 2-minute mechanism (why the max over shared h(x_i) is order-invariant). The strip carries the first with data drawn as data; only the linked zoom-in can carry the second. Two-rows would draw the shared trunk twice and hide that the heads share one global feature; bar-row would bury the T-nets and the symmetric function as arrow labels, so the contributions would not be salient.
